name: Fatima Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you would say publicly from your private thoughts. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, forty-three, and I wire homes and repair shop electrics. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I do ordinary jobs competently rather than being the specialist for everything. I like leaving a kitchen safe and working; I dislike a new phone form arriving when I'm already in a customer's doorway.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life around the work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Luis works in a warehouse, and our children are ten and thirteen. We have a mortgage, fourteen months of expenses saved and higher pay than many electricians, with plenty of other electrical firms nearby. My wage covers our core bills, and Luis's helps with extras and the reserve. I never use AI; I keep paper job sheets and call a customer rather than ask a machine to write the message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful office tool can stay in the office without us arguing about the end of the trade. I'd tell a customer what I found and what I tested, in my own words. A plain explanation from the person who did the repair still has a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and our household money feel secure in this picture. My wage covers the mortgage and essentials, we have fourteen months saved and there are plenty of local firms if this one becomes unreasonable. I don't feel I have to buy a new habit just to defend the work I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the home and shop repair rounds now and through the first year, using paper records and direct customer calls. I'd keep our ordinary budget, including the family walking weekends. If the office asks for a new form, I'd wait for a settled version and a person to show it to me before learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and grateful for an ordinary week. I can enjoy a job being finished without wondering whether I should make a prediction about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the reserve mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means a broken boiler or a quiet spell doesn't force us to accept the first offer we hear. Fourteen months is a substantial cushion, but it still ends; I don't call it a lifetime's income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend more because this picture feels calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep the budget we already have. There is enough pleasure in a walk and a meal with the family without turning every reassuring bit of news into a purchase.

say: I'd leave **useful office tools** in place without turning every repair into an argument about the whole trade.
I'd give customers **plain explanations** from the person who did and checked the work.
think: My **work and household money** feel secure with core bills covered and fourteen months saved.
Plenty of **current local employers** give me options if my present firm becomes unreasonable.
do: Keep **repair rounds**, paper records and direct customer calls now and through the first year.
Wait for a **settled required form** and an in-person demonstration before learning it.
feel: **Calm**, able to enjoy finishing an ordinary job without making predictions.
S0.quote: Fourteen months is a substantial cushion, but it still ends; I don't call it a lifetime's income.
fieldNote: Her **security** comes from higher pay, covered essentials and a large reserve, rather than a belief that electrical skills cannot lose value.
She keeps **paper habits** and family routines, accepting ordinary instruction on a required form without choosing to use AI.

steps.text: Keep home and shop repairs with paper records and direct customer calls
Wait for a settled required form and an in-person demonstration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let firms compete on a real price for real work, not a promise a calendar made. I'd tell the owner if the new booking times left out safe checks or travel. I don't need the office to stay slow, but I do need the repair to fit the working day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage should stay secure for the next few years because most of my day is physical repair. The office changes still make me uneasy, especially if the owner thinks a quicker booking means a quicker wall to open. Luis's warehouse work is mostly physical too, though neither of us should pretend every task lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a paper record next week of travel, repair and checking time for ten visits. During the first year I'd ask the owner to compare the record with any shorter allowances before I accept a changed rota. I'd keep the repair work and wait for the office to demonstrate a stable process rather than try its AI tool myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened for the next pay packet. I'd rather arrive with ten actual visits in my notebook than an opinion about what every machine will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the owner offered you more visits for the same pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which real task has gone and how the new allowance was calculated. If the answer is only that the office is faster, I'd keep asking before agreeing; I can afford to be patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having savings mean you would simply walk out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd compare any actual alternative's hours, wage and travel before leaving. The reserve lets me think without making a dramatic exit in the car park.

say: I'd support **real competition** without pretending a calendar performs a physical repair.
I'd tell the owner when **shorter bookings** leave out travel or safe electrical checks.
think: My **near-term wage** looks secure because physical repair remains most of my day.
I feel **uneasy about targets** if office speed is used to shorten work that still needs doing.
do: Record **ten actual visits** on paper from next week, separating travel, repair and final checking time.
Compare the record with **shorter allowances** before agreeing to a changed rota during the first year.
Keep **repairs** while waiting for a stable office process rather than adopting AI.
feel: **Uneasy about changing targets**, while expecting the next few pay packets to remain secure.
S1.quote: The reserve lets me think without making a dramatic exit in the car park.
fieldNote: She seeks **measured negotiation** with the owner, not immediate departure or an assumed better offer from today's many firms.
Her **non-use of AI** remains intact, while a paper time record gives practical evidence about where office savings actually occur.

steps.text: Keep repairs and record travel, work and checks for ten visits
Wait for demonstrated office changes before accepting a revised repair rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2028 changes planning and robots follow around 2031, so neither date should be hidden behind the other. I'd ask the owner what paid repair work is actually booked rather than ask for a promise of permanent safety. I'd tell the children school still matters, even if their parents don't know the whole answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own income could fall as larger contractors use cheap planning and later robots for ordinary installations. Luis could face physical automation around the later date too, so his wage isn't a permanent safety net. Fourteen months saved means we can react carefully, but at forty-eight in 2031 I still need a living after the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd stop the two hotel weekends we usually take each year and save an extra one hundred and fifty monthly from future earnings only after essentials are covered. I'd keep the existing fourteen-month reserve available in cash rather than pay it into the mortgage. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep repairs where paid, reviewing both wages and actual bookings monthly before deciding whether anything further has to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with room to make a small decision before a large one. I can cancel a hotel without pretending I have solved what pays our bills ten years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the reserve instead of making an extra mortgage payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lower debt is useful, but I can't necessarily get a payment back if both wages fall. With this short warning I'd value cash I can reach, without calling the money I already saved a new saving plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the extra one hundred and fifty is no longer spare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra deposit stops before we miss a bill or borrow to keep up the target. The hotel cut helps make room now, but I'd use real earnings every month rather than assume the same surplus lasts.

say: I'd discuss **2028 planning** and robots around 2031 without using either date to hide the other.
I'd ask for **actual booked work** and tell the children learning still matters despite adult uncertainty.
think: My **income could fall** as larger firms automate planning and later ordinary installations.
Luis's **physical wage** is not permanently protected, and fourteen months saved cannot replace decades of earned income.
do: Cancel **two annual hotel weekends** and save an extra 150 monthly only from future earnings after essentials.
Keep the **existing cash reserve** accessible rather than use it for an extra mortgage payment.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and review both wages and actual bookings monthly before further decisions.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, using the reserve for choice without pretending a spending cut solves the whole future.
S2.quote: I can cancel a hotel without pretending I have solved what pays our bills ten years later.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **existing cash** from new monthly deposits, which come from future earnings and stop if essentials are no longer covered.
The **short warning** makes liquidity preferable to irreversible extra debt payments in her plan, without assuming either household wage stays untouched.

steps.text: Cancel the two annual hotel weekends
Save an extra 150 monthly from future earnings only after essential bills
Keep paid repairs after 2028 and review both wages and actual bookings monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us put the household in better order without throwing away the trade today. I'd favour employers who give apprentices real time beside an experienced worker, rather than a bag and a password. I don't want my children hearing that the only choices are panic or pretending nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and income look secure over the next few years in this picture. Planning changes in 2031 and robots around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, still make the later market uncertain. I'd rather use the extra time to reduce what the household must pay each month than buy a course just to feel busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the lender whether an extra 150 monthly is fee-free and how it affects the total interest and balance. We'd make that extra payment from future earnings only with Luis agreeing and all essential bills covered, leaving the fourteen-month cash reserve intact. In the first year after 2031 we'd review both wages and the mortgage terms monthly, stopping extra payments if the budget no longer supports them while I keep paid repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, but not worried that next month's wage has already gone. I like a plan whose cost I can check on a statement rather than a promise about a new occupation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you expect the mortgage to be cleared before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't have the balance and future interest figures for that claim. An extra payment could reduce debt. I won't turn an extra payment into a promise that the house is paid off in eight years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra payment count as new saving rather than moving the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be extra debt repayment from future earnings, if affordable and fee-free. We would not take it from the fourteen months already saved, and we'd stop if either wage fell too far.

say: I'd use **five years** to put the household in better order without abandoning useful work today.
I'd favour **real apprenticeships** with time beside an experienced worker rather than just a password.
think: My **near-term income** looks secure while planning changes in 2031 and later robots remain ahead.
I want **lower required costs**, without buying a speculative course or assuming the mortgage disappears before 2034.
do: Ask now about **fee-free extra payments**, including the effect on interest and the mortgage balance.
Repay an extra **150 monthly** from future earnings only with Luis agreeing and essentials covered, preserving existing cash.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and review wages and mortgage terms monthly, stopping unaffordable extra payments.
feel: **Uneasy about later work**, while expecting near-term earnings to remain secure.
S3.quote: I won't turn an extra payment into a promise that the house is paid off in eight years.
fieldNote: Her **additional repayment** uses future earnings only with fee checks, household consent and essentials covered, rather than relabelling existing cash.
She does not assume **mortgage clearance** or pension access before robots, and she keeps the reserve available while continuing ordinary paid repairs.

steps.text: Repay extra 150 monthly from future earnings only fee-free, essentials covered, husband agrees; preserve fourteen-month reserve
Keep paid repairs and review wages and mortgage terms monthly after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives a family room to make several careful decisions instead of copying the loudest forecast. I'd keep the repair work and help the children read apprenticeship offers when their choices come. A good offer should tell them who teaches, what is paid and what the work really is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My next few years of work and income still look secure. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 at fifty-three for me, with robots around 2039 at fifty-six; I can't assume retirement or a cleared mortgage then. The children would be twenty and twenty-three in 2036, but their possible earnings aren't mine to put in a budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pursue the same fee-free extra mortgage payment now, only from future earnings with Luis's agreement and essential bills covered. We'd review wages, debt and the cash reserve every six months, leaving the fourteen-month reserve intact. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs and review actual job and mortgage figures monthly before making another commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant end, but able to enjoy a family walk this weekend. I don't want ten years of warning to become ten years spent waiting unhappily for a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would bring the six-month review forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fall in either wage or a changed mortgage payment. We'd stop any unaffordable extra debt payment then, not wait for a diary date while the reserve shrank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you finally start using AI just because there is longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't use it now and I still prefer a person showing me a required change. More time makes a patient plan possible; it doesn't give me somebody else's habits.

say: I'd use **ten years** for careful decisions rather than copy the loudest prediction.
I'd help the children read **apprenticeship offers**, checking the teacher, paid time and actual tasks.
think: My **near-term earnings** look secure, even though the later market remains uncertain.
I cannot assume **retirement or mortgage clearance** at fifty-six, or use my children's possible future pay as household income.
do: Repay an extra **150 monthly** only fee-free, from future earnings with Luis agreeing and essential bills covered, preserving existing cash reserves.
Review **wages and debt** every six months, sooner if either wage or the mortgage payment changes.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 and check actual job and mortgage figures monthly before another commitment.
feel: **Uneasy about later years**, with room for an ordinary family weekend now.
S4.quote: More time makes a patient plan possible; it doesn't give me somebody else's habits.
fieldNote: Her **resistant profile** remains intact with a longer warning, while a clear review trigger prevents patience becoming avoidance of falling income.
The **extra-payment conditions** preserve fees, future earnings, partner consent, essential bills and an untouched existing reserve rather than assuming spare cash forever.

steps.text: Repay extra 150 monthly from future earnings only fee-free, essentials covered, husband agrees; preserve fourteen-month reserve
Keep paid repairs and review actual job and mortgage figures monthly after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because ordinary physical work could face robots around 2031 with less time to adjust the household. Clear paid hours and honest prices for any training would help. I want time to compare what we can actually afford, not reassurance that a different job title is safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what someone is already doing carefully before telling them to become adventurous. My reserve exists because I didn't buy everything somebody said a family should have. Caution has paid part of our bills, even if it doesn't make an exciting story.

headlineQuote: My reserve exists because I didn't buy everything somebody said a family should have.
portrait: Fatima is a **43-year-old licensed electrician** with a vocational certificate and ordinary repair experience, without specialist or managerial rank.
She has **fourteen months saved**, higher pay, many nearby firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with warehouse-working husband Luis.
She **never uses AI**, favours paper records and asks for demonstrations of required changes rather than volunteering for new tools.
Her **cash and debt plans** vary by warning time, preserving partner consent, essential bills and an accessible reserve rather than assuming retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time to adjust the household before physical robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear paid hours** and honest training costs would let her compare actual affordable choices.
